documents: g22_W4221124205.pdf: published paper, Bromhead et al. 2022, Journal of Petroleum Geology 45(2), pp. 119-162 (PDF only; no review file, discussion or earlier version supplied)

entry.evidence: However, an increase in both spatial and temporal resolution is required for purposes of exploration and field appraisal.

steps.action: The authors note that plate-scale studies and palaeogeographic maps are scarce and coarse, and set the aim of producing data-supported GDE maps at plate scale within a high-resolution sequence stratigraphic framework.
steps.quote: [...] aims to provide a series of data-supported gross depositional environment (GDE) maps

steps.action: They compile published well logs, outcrop logs, sparse 2D seismic, biostratigraphic, isotope, petrographic, geochemical and hydrocarbon-occurrence data from the public domain.
steps.quote: a stratigraphic dataset consisting of 626 published wells and 176 published outcrop sections

steps.action: They adopt the Arabian Plate Sequence Stratigraphic Model of Sharland et al. (2001), as updated by Davies et al. (2002) and van Buchem et al. (2011), as the framework.
steps.quote: derived from the Arabian Plate Sequence Stratigraphic model of Sharland et al. (2001)

steps.action: They apply the model first to age-constrained sections and then correlate it into the other sections by wireline log patterns and facies changes, giving every interpreted surface a proxy age; regional transects, GDE maps and isopachs follow from this.
steps.quote: the application of the sequence stratigraphic model provides a proxy age attribution for each sequence stratigraphic surface

steps.action: They refine the Sharland et al. framework by adding the Tu1 and Tu2 sequences within the Turonian, with Tu2 treated as a division within K150.
steps.quote: this study recognizes two additional sequences within the Turonian

steps.action: They calibrate the ages of the sequence surfaces at the Natih Formation type outcrop in Oman, using published ammonite, foraminiferal and d13C events (Fig. 4), and note uncertain zones and disputed identifications.
steps.quote: The outcrops represent an excellent location for the age calibration of the mid-Cretaceous sequences (Fig. 4)

steps.action: They frame intrashelf basin development with two end-member conceptual models (Fig. 5, Table 1): a symmetric basin with minor siliciclastic input and an asymmetric basin with significant siliciclastic input. The models build on van Buchem/Razin and on Davies et al.
steps.quote: Herein, we consider the development of Cenomanian–Turonian intrashelf basins in terms of these two end-member models

steps.action: They compare their dip-oriented Iraq correlations (Figs 7, 8) with earlier interpretations, reinterpret the western wells as a mixed homoclinal ramp, and so reduce the areal extent of the Najaf basin.
steps.quote: tend to challenge the interpretations of Aqrawi and Horbury (2008)

steps.action: They infer a K140 intrashelf basin in the Rub' al Khali of Saudi Arabia from elevated gamma-ray and molybdenum responses in published chemostratigraphic well data.
steps.quote: organic-rich intrashelf basin facies are interpreted to occur based on elevated gamma-ray log responses

steps.action: They state the published rival placements and settings of the Kifl Formation: below the mid-Turonian unconformity, in an isolated restricted basin or in an evaporitic lagoon behind the Mishrif margin.
steps.quote: Deposition of the Kifl Formation has been interpreted to have occurred in an isolated, restricted basin

steps.action: They reject a pre-unconformity Kifl on preservation grounds and assign it to early transgressive facies above the K150 SB.
steps.quote: it seems unlikely that the predominantly evaporitic Kifl Formation could have been preserved

steps.action: They compare the sequence isopach maps with the GDE maps (Fig. 13) to describe how accommodation evolved under sea-level, palaeogeographic and tectonic controls.
steps.quote: Comparing sequence isopach maps and GDE maps (Fig. 13) demonstrates the evolution of accommodation space

steps.action: They reject linking Cenomanian palaeohigh reactivation in the Dezful Embayment to compression, because the K130 and Tu1 unconformities pre-date the active-margin transition.
steps.quote: it seems likely that only the mid-Turonian unconformity is associated with the compressional phase

steps.action: They compare the preservation pattern in Fars Province: Cenomanian stratigraphy is missing, while the underlying Albian is complete with limited thickness variation.
steps.quote: variable preservation beneath the mid-Turonian unconformity is limited to the Cenomanian and does not extend into the Albian

steps.action: They favour Cenomanian non-deposition on an active structural high over later mid-Turonian erosion, because erosion would be expected to cut into the Albian.
steps.quote: may be related to non-deposition during the Cenomanian across an active structural high

steps.action: They compile published Mishrif porosity-permeability data by depositional facies (Fig. 15) to show the facies control on reservoir quality that the GDE-based screening relies on.
steps.quote: This is demonstrated in Fig. 15 which shows porosity-permeability data taken from the Mishrif Formation

steps.action: They screen for the subcrop play by mapping preservation limits onto each GDE surface and combining these with HST reservoir facies and karst prediction (Fig. 17).
steps.quote: By mapping the preservation limits on each GDE map surface, the maps can be processed to give the subcrop extent within each sequence.

steps.action: They check the screening output against the distribution of producing Cenomanian–Turonian fields; six known trends reconcile, and a frontier area in the Rub' al Khali is high-graded.
steps.quote: The results of the subcrop screening (Fig. 17) show trends which are consistent with the distribution of fields producing from Cenomanian–Turonian reservoirs

steps.action: They keep the plate-scale framework, the symmetric/asymmetric controls on petroleum system elements, and the subcrop play as conclusions.
steps.quote: three Cenomanian sequences can be correlated with confidence at the scale of the Arabian Plate

end.claim: A plate-wide, age-attributed sequence stratigraphic framework (K110–Tu2) with MFS/HST/LST GDE and isopach maps reconstructs Cenomanian–Turonian palaeogeography; it shows that petroleum system elements differ between symmetric and asymmetric intrashelf basins and that a subcrop play beneath the K150 SB is regionally predictable.

decisive_move.sentence: Applying the age-calibrated sequence model to all 802 published sections, which gives proxy ages to every surface regardless of data quality, creates the plate-scale dataset on which every map and conclusion rests.

gates.evidence: All data were compiled from the published literature without a hypothesis directing acquisition (p. 120, 153). The only test the main product could have failed is the comparison of subcrop screening with producing-field trends (p. 150), and hydrocarbon-occurrence data were among the inputs (p. 120). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

novelty_claims.quote: These maps characterize the palaeogeography at a previously unprecedented resolution and scale
this study recognizes two additional sequences within the Turonian
This model has achieved a stratigraphic resolution that is beyond previously published maps
The sequence attributed plate-scale dataset used in this study is unique and offers some important new insights

limits: Only the published paper was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the acknowledgements say referees improved early drafts, but what changed is unknown. The paper does not say how correlations were picked, how ambiguous ties were resolved, or how map boundaries were interpolated between data points. No uncertainty is attached to the GDE or isopach maps. The authors note that the quality and completeness of public-domain sections are highly variable. There are no robustness or sensitivity tests. The field-distribution check (p. 150) is not independent, because the hydrocarbon-occurrence dataset was an input (inference). Sub-claims and their statuses: the Najaf basin areal reduction is best_explanation; the Kifl Formation placement above the K150 SB is best_explanation, argued on preservation grounds only; the Tu1 SB assignment in the Sarvak is acknowledged as possibly older (K140 SB), so it is unresolved; the extension of the Mishrif into the earliest Turonian is an inference from the model without biostratigraphic support (p. 140); the Rub' al Khali exploration opportunity is an unscored prediction (none); Fars non-deposition versus erosion is best_explanation. Much of the age control and many key observations are cited from other workers rather than performed here.

disagreements.target: Aqrawi and Horbury (2008); Aqrawi et al. (2010), extent of the Najaf intrashelf basin
disagreements.support: Their dip-oriented well correlations reinterpret the western wells as a mixed carbonate-siliciclastic homoclinal ramp, which shrinks the basin.
disagreements.quote: tend to challenge the interpretations of Aqrawi and Horbury (2008)

disagreements.target: Conventional placement of the Kifl Formation below the mid-Turonian unconformity (Aqrawi et al., 2010; Mahdi and Aqrawi, 2014; [...]
disagreements.support: An evaporitic unit is unlikely to have survived a ~5 Ma unconformity, and its association with Laffan-like facies in Basrah supports a post-uplift position.
disagreements.quote: The alternative interpretation presented here assigns the Kifl Formation to above the mid-Turonian regional unconformity (K150 SB).

disagreements.target: Mehrabi and Rahimpour-Bonab (2014), Cenomanian palaeohigh reactivation by compression
disagreements.support: The K130 and Tu1 unconformities pre-date the active-margin transition at the K150 SB (Sharland et al., 2001).
disagreements.quote: However, the mid-Cenomanian (K130 SB) and Cenomanian–Turonian boundary (probable Tu1 SB) unconformities pre-date the transition to an active margin

disagreements.target: Omidvar et al. (2014), Turonian age of the upper Sarvak assemblage zone
disagreements.support: They cite Schlagintweit and Yazdi-Moghadam (2021), who show that M. apenninica occurs in Cenomanian strata.
disagreements.quote: leaving the age of this zone open to question

disagreements.target: van Buchem et al. (2002), late Turonian Coilopoceras requienianum near the top of the Natih
disagreements.support: A personal communication suggests the specimen may be early–middle Turonian Choffaticeras.
disagreements.quote: but this has been disputed (Luc Bulot, pers. comm. 2021)

disagreements.target: Early Cenomanian age calibration from benthic foraminifera in the upper Natih E (e.g. Simmons and Hart, 1987)
disagreements.support: They cite later work showing that the fauna is endemic and so gives no direct age calibration.
disagreements.quote: much of the distinctive benthic foraminifera fauna in the uppermost Natih E is in fact endemic

disagreements.target: Previous plate-scale palaeogeographic maps (Murris, 1980; Burchette, 1993; Ziegler, 2001)
disagreements.support: These maps give useful context but lack the spatial and temporal resolution needed for exploration.
disagreements.quote: However, an increase in both spatial and temporal resolution is required for purposes of exploration and field appraisal.

disagreements.target: Fault compartmentalization as the explanation of crest-shallow oil-water contacts (Abteymur, Nahr Umr)
disagreements.support: No faulting is seen on seismic and petrophysics shows a single free-water level, so a facies-controlled pore-system model is viable.
disagreements.quote: a viable alternative model places microporous rocks at the crests of the structures and macroporous rocks on the flanks
